Caleb Marsh gave him the steadier shape at the other end, compact early, patient through the first line changes, and useful enough in the singles that even quiet overs did not fully belong to the fielding side. Once Nathan went, the innings collapsed into scattered dismissals and tiny partnerships. Owen Mercer was left not out, but by then the match had long since stopped being a chase. Jack Bennett’s two wickets made sure the middle never stabilized, Noah Price’s three broke the lower order, and Connor Wells finished it with very little ceremony. Noah Hart was the correct Player of the Match because his unbeaten hundred was not decorative. It was the innings that gave Harborfield scale, safety, and control. Mason Hart turned that advantage into a rout with the ball, but the match’s main structure came from Noah’s ability to stay through every important batting phase and make the final margin feel inevitable. Harborfield won by 196 runs, and the scoreline matched the day: one side built properly, the other never escaped the first spell.

When the bowlers went defensive, he found the single early and the boundary late. When they missed full, he drove straight. When they dragged short, he was ready to hit square or over midwicket. The stand with Graham reached 100, and that was the decisive passage of the first innings because it took Ridgefield from a good but vulnerable 203 for 5 to 303 for 6. Dylan Grant eventually removed Marcus, and soon after Graham also went, but the match had already moved. Hayden Brooks added a brief 11, Isaac Lane stayed unbeaten with 9, Jordan Dale helped finish the last over, and Ridgefield closed on 337 for 8. Southport’s bowling had its moments. Logan Reed’s two wickets created the middle squeeze. Caleb Frost’s spell was the most disciplined of the main options. Dylan Grant dismissed Marcus and Graham, which gave the figures late respectability. Connor Hale got the first breakthrough. Aiden Ford closed off Hayden. Yet Southport never managed to own two phases in a row. Every time they got a wicket, Ridgefield found another structure, and every time they seemed close to control, Marcus Ward changed the cost of the next over. Chasing 338, Southport needed a start that would make the target feel like a sequence rather than a mountain, and for the first nine overs they gave themselves exactly that. Ethan Moore and Liam Hughes came out with intent, Ethan especially sharp through the off side, getting to 31 from 30 and putting early pressure back onto Kyle Mercer and Elliott Hayes. Kyle Mercer removed Ethan, and although Noah Reed helped Liam push the score along briefly, Isaac Lane’s lbw against Noah stopped that second stand before it could become meaningful. The chase was still alive, though, because Liam Hughes and Owen Clarke then produced Southport’s best passage of the innings. From 163 for 4 to 165 for 5, the innings moved from possible chase into pressure management, and Ridgefield sensed it immediately. Mason Stone and Logan Reed tried to patch something together, Mason making 11 and Logan 16, but Hayden Brooks broke both pieces before they could become more than small resistance. Aiden Ford briefly gave the reply a spark with two sixes in his 12, but Jordan Dale removed him too, and that was the last moment where Southport looked capable of pushing back with any violence. Connor Hale stayed around, but his unbeaten 5 from 25 was survival rather than threat, and once Kyle Mercer bowled Dylan Grant and Isaac Lane finished Parker Lane, Southport were all out for 222 in 41.2 overs. Kyle Mercer broke the opening and later cut off Dylan Grant. Isaac Lane took Noah Reed and the final wicket. Graham Holt removed Caleb Frost at a point where Southport still needed a middle-order platform. Hayden Brooks took Mason Stone and Logan Reed, which stopped the lower middle from creating another phase. Jordan Dale was the most decisive in the chase’s central corridor, removing Liam Hughes, Owen Clarke, and Aiden Ford, the three batters most capable of changing either the rhythm or the emotional direction of the pursuit. Adrian Cole and Brandon Vale gave them the start. Cameron Stone bridged the first transition. Marcus Ward rescued and then dominated the vulnerable middle. Everything that followed, including Southport’s chase starting well and then fading under the weight of the target, was downstream of that innings.

Greenfield Park in the East Midlands had that slightly false calm at the start, the kind of afternoon where a captain can win the toss, choose to bat, and still discover within a few overs that the match has already shifted into damage control, and that was exactly what happened to Ridgefield, because Eastport’s new-ball pair struck early enough and accurately enough to make the innings feel broken before it had even reached its first real decision point. Noah Carter went almost immediately, pushing at Ryan Cole and giving Owen Hart the catch before the batting side had a run from the bat, and Mason Blake’s run-out shortly after made the opening damage feel even worse because it was not just good bowling now, it was pressure turning into poor running. Ethan Ward tried to stitch the start together with a few controlled strokes, but Ryan Cole returned to remove him as well, and when Caleb Moore was bowled by Isaac Bell, Ridgefield were twenty-three for four and already searching for rescue rather than platform. That early passage is the important foundation of the match, because every later Ridgefield run had to be understood against it. They were never building freely. They were trying to make a damaged innings respectable. Daniel Price and Oliver Grant did the first part of that work, adding twenty-seven and at least giving the innings a middle, Oliver striking one clean six and Daniel playing the steadier hand, but Isaac Bell broke that stand before it could become a real turn, and Ridgefield were still only halfway to safety when Jacob Ellis arrived as the one batter who finally changed the tone. Jacob’s forty-one from thirty-one was the only innings in the card that looked capable of taking Eastport out of their comfortable rhythm. He came in after the fifth wicket, hit with clearer intent than anyone before him, and with Daniel first, then Henry Brooks, then Logan Hayes, he kept dragging the total into a range that Eastport would at least have to chase properly. His stand with Daniel was worth twenty-two, then another small one with Henry kept the innings from folding, and the partnership with Logan was the one that made 118 possible rather than something down near a hundred. Felix Stone’s spell through this phase was decisive, because he did not simply collect tail-end wickets after the damage was done. He removed Daniel Price, then Henry Brooks, then Jacob Ellis, and each wicket arrived at a point when Ridgefield were trying to stretch the recovery into something more useful. That is why his three for eighteen mattered so much. It cut the innings off before Jacob could fully cash in. Logan Hayes and the last pair did squeeze out a few more, helped by late extras, and Sam Allen’s wicket on 118 closed the card with one ball still unused in the nineteenth over, but the innings never escaped its original wound. Eastport had distributed the work well: Ryan Cole struck twice at the top, Isaac Bell stopped the first repair, Felix controlled the most important middle-lower phase, and Nathan King cleaned up the final pair. Ridgefield’s 118 was not a surrender, because Jacob had given it some resistance and the tail had fought for scraps, but it was still a total built from a collapse, not from a plan. Eastport’s chase then began with enough trouble to keep the game honest. Leo Grant fell almost immediately, caught behind off Peter Shaw, and Paul Jackson followed soon after, the same bowler finding the edge again, so at sixteen for two the target briefly looked heavier than it had at the interval. That is where Felix Stone completed the second half of his match. He did not treat the chase as if the low target gave him permission to be careless. He first rebuilt with Mark Harris, who made eighteen from sixteen and gave Eastport the brisk support they needed after two early wickets, then carried the innings into control with Brian Martin. The stand with Mark was worth thirty-four and moved Eastport out of the opening wobble. The stand with Brian was even more important because it took the score to ninety-five and turned the chase from a contest into a managed finish. Brian’s twenty-one was not large, but it arrived in the right tempo, just enough boundary pressure to stop Ridgefield from crowding Felix, just enough composure to keep the required rate from becoming a talking point. When Henry Brooks eventually removed Brian, Eastport still needed only a small closing hand, and Kevin Young supplied it immediately, hitting cleanly enough in his short unbeaten ten to make sure the chase did not drift. Felix stayed there to the end, unbeaten on fifty-eight from forty-four, and the texture of that innings is what makes the player-of-the-match call straightforward. He was not only the top scorer in the chase. He was the batter who absorbed the only early danger, organized both major partnerships, and finished the job without allowing Ridgefield one final squeeze. Ridgefield’s bowlers had useful moments, especially Peter Shaw with the two early wickets and Thomas Wilson’s tidy spell in the middle, but they never had the cluster they needed after Felix settled. Logan Hayes removed Mark Harris, Henry Brooks removed Brian Martin, yet each wicket came after Eastport had already moved the chase into a safer lane. The contrast between the two innings is therefore clean. Ridgefield lost early wickets and had to rebuild through one main hand; Eastport lost early wickets too, but their main hand stayed longer, controlled more of the chase, and had enough support around him to prevent the innings from becoming fragmented. Ridgefield’s recovery was brave but limited. Eastport’s response was smaller in drama and larger in control. The scoreboard follows that logic: Ridgefield 118 all out after a top-order failure and a Jacob Ellis rescue; Eastport 121 for four after Felix Stone turned a brief wobble into a six-wicket match. The match was decided by which side handled instability better, and Eastport handled it better in both halves.

At Westhaven Youth Cricket Ground in Meridian, Ridgefield against Coastline played out like one of those fifty-over youth matches where the early score almost lies to you, because Ridgefield won the toss, chose to bat, and for a long opening stretch seemed to have built enough calm to make the innings work, only for Coastline’s bowlers to keep peeling away the structure until a useful platform turned into a small target and a chase that briefly looked nervous became controlled by one decisive middle partnership. Owen Hart and Leo Mercer began with the right idea for the format, not rushing the new ball, not trying to force a high tempo on a surface that was clearly rewarding straight bowling and patience, and their stand of 52 gave Ridgefield the kind of first act a batting side wants after electing to set a score. Owen was the proper hand in that partnership, moving with more confidence, finding the rope when anything sat up, and playing with enough shape to suggest he might carry the innings deep. Leo was far more restrained, making 14 from 50, but his occupation still mattered because Ridgefield were at least keeping wickets intact. Then the match changed. Ethan Brooks removed Leo, Noah Reed quickly cut off Carter Shaw and Ben Porter, and from 52 without loss the innings slid into a sequence of restarts that never became a second platform. Owen tried to keep the card alive, reaching 46 from 74, but Aaron Vale got through him at 69 and that was the hinge of the first innings, because the one batter who had understood the day was gone before the score had truly become safe. Gavin Lane followed without moving the total, Alec Stone’s little boundary hand ended almost as soon as it began, Adrian Vale was bowled, Nolan Reed was taken by the same bowler, and Isaac Ford could not give Jason Brook the support he needed. Jason’s 27 from 42 was valuable in the lower order because it dragged Ridgefield from the edge of embarrassment toward something at least defendable, and the last stand with Aiden Frost gave them a few more runs before Ethan Brooks finished it, but 112 all out in 40.4 overs was still well short of what the opening stand had promised. Coastline’s bowling was not built on one flashy over alone. Mason Cross and Noah Reed broke the first wave of rebuilding, Ethan Brooks struck at the start and end of the innings, and Aaron Vale’s 10 overs for 11 with four wickets gave the whole card its decisive shape. His spell mattered because it removed Owen Hart and then closed down the tail before Ridgefield could crawl into the 130s, which is why the player-of-the-match call fits the match rather than just the scorebook. Chasing 113, Coastline began quickly enough to suggest a routine finish, with Miles Kane playing the most positive early shots in a 32-run opening stand, but Sandgate-style pressure appeared for a moment when Ben Porter changed the tone. Miles fell first, Logan Pierce was bowled soon after by Carter Shaw, and Ethan Brooks was caught with the score only 43, so Coastline were three down before the chase had fully settled. That was Ridgefield’s best chance, and for a few overs the small target did begin to feel a little larger. Cole Grant and Tyler Brook removed that tension by batting the situation rather than the scoreboard. Cole was the more assured player, making 43 from 40 with five fours and a six, and he understood that Coastline did not need a reckless counterattack; they needed one batter to hold the chase together while the target kept shrinking. Tyler Brook was quieter but essential, staying unbeaten on 20 from 36 and refusing to let Ben Porter’s spell become a real collapse. Their fourth-wicket stand of 60 took Coastline from 43 for 3 to 103 for 4, and by the time Cole finally fell, the game had already been reduced to a handful of calm runs rather than a dangerous finish. Aaron Vale then joined Tyler and, fittingly, helped close the match he had defined with the ball, finishing unbeaten as Coastline reached 114 for 4 in 22.5 overs. Ridgefield had one genuine innings from Owen, a small lower-order fight from Jason, and a strong defensive burst from Ben Porter, but they never recovered from the collapse that followed their opening stand. Coastline were sharper where the match actually turned: Aaron Vale broke the first innings, Cole Grant rebuilt the chase, and Tyler Brook stayed long enough to make sure the early wobble did not become a final twist. The result therefore lands cleanly: Ridgefield 112 all out after wasting a stable start, Coastline 114 for 4 after one brief scare and one mature partnership, a six-wicket win built through bowling control first and chase management second.
